title: Meeting Spot With the Least Total Walking
statement:
A city is a grid of blocks. grid[r][c] is 1 if a friend lives on that block and 0 otherwise. Everyone walks along the streets, so going from (r1, c1) to (r2, c2) costs |r1 − r2| + |c1 − c2|.

The friends want to meet on one block, any block of the grid, including one where someone lives. Return the smallest possible sum of everyone's walking distance.

examples.why: Meet at (2, 1): the friend at (0, 1) walks 2, the two at the bottom walk 1 each.
Meet at column 1: 1 + 0 + 5. The average column is about 2.3, and meeting at column 2 costs 2 + 1 + 4 = 7. The middle friend beats the average.
With two friends, any block between them costs the same 3.

hints: The cost splits into a row part and a column part that do not affect each other. Solve each one on its own.
On a single line, which point minimises the sum of distances to a set of points? It is not the average.

It is the median. Collect the rows of all friends in sorted order (a row-by-row scan gives that for free) and the columns too (scan column by column). Then sum the distances to the median, or pair the outermost points from both ends.

explain.intuition:
Manhattan distance is just row distance plus column distance, and the meeting row does not change the column cost. So the 2D problem is two 1D problems: pick a row that minimises the total row distance, and separately a column.

On a line, the best point is the median. Stand anywhere and move one step right: everyone to your right gets one step closer and everyone to your left one step farther. That pays off while more people are on your right, and stops paying off exactly at the middle person. The average gets pulled towards outliers, as the second example shows; the median does not care how far away they are.
steps: Scan the grid row by row and record the row of each friend. These come out sorted.
Scan column by column and record the column of each friend. Also sorted.
For each list, walk two pointers in from both ends and add list[hi] − list[lo]. Every outer pair contributes exactly that much whatever median you pick.
Return the sum of the two totals.
pitfalls: Meeting at the average position. It is the answer for squared distances, not for walking distances.
Sorting the coordinates with a comparison sort without needing to: scanning in the right order gives sorted lists for free.
Trying every block and summing distances. With 40 000 blocks and up to 40 000 friends that is over a billion steps.

solutions.title: Try every block
solutions.idea: For each block, add up everyone's distance to it and keep the smallest total.

solutions.title: Median of rows and of columns
solutions.idea: Split the cost into rows and columns. Gather each coordinate in sorted order by scanning, then pair the outermost points: each pair adds their gap.

followups: Some blocks are walls that nobody can cross. Why does the median trick break, and what would you do instead?
Each friend has a weight (how many people live there). How do you find a weighted median?
